reconcile.connective: Defenders read the repentance as anthropopathic: the words describe a change in God's dealings with corrupted humanity, not a reversal of his mind or his original verdict.

discrepancy.connective: Thomas Paine pressed exactly this tension, charging that a God who pronounces his world finished and 'very good' yet later drowns it and repents of having made it is depicted as changeable, not the unchangeable Being creation itself suggests.

skeptic.name: Thomas Paine
skeptic.work: Letters Concerning The Age of Reason
skeptic.attribution: Thomas Paine (d. 1809), Letters Concerning The Age of Reason (1797)

excerpts.excerpt_text: It does not imply any change of God's mind; for he is in one mind, and who can turn him? With him there is not variableness. But it expressed a change of his way. … so that the change was in man, not in God.
excerpts.on_tension_rationale: Directly answers the satisfaction-to-regret tension: the Gen 6:6 'repentance' is read as a changed dealing with apostate humanity, not a reversal of the Gen 1:31 verdict or of God's mind. Strongest single harmonization on the row; parity-capped to one because the discrepancy pole carries one named-skeptic connective.

pd_work.resource: John Haley, An Examination of the Alleged Discrepancies of the Bible (1874)
pd_work.author: John Haley
pd_work.note: Haley's doctrinal-discrepancies section treats the passages on God's repentance (incl. Gen 6:6) against divine immutability, the exact mechanism of this tension.
